Trans-Canada Highway Act

I am trying to do a little fishing and find out what the intention of the government is with respect to a second trans-Canada highway but I am getting nowhere. The Prime Minister said in the house, as found on page 1839 of Hansard:
The question of another trans-Canada highway has not heen discussed with the provinces particularly.
I do not know whether he means that it has not been discussed with the provinces at all or whether particular provinces have not been included in the discussions. We all know that many of the comments made by the Prime Minister can be taken a number of ways. We are very disappointed and I am sure the people who have made representations are disappointed that nothing is going to happen with respect to a second trans-Canada highway until the first one is completed. I assume that means nothing will happen until the last mile in the last province is completed, whether that be some three years from now as is expected or whether it be five or ten years from now which will mean that the government will have to come back in a few years and ask for another extension.
I suggest to the minister and the government that this is most unfair because the financial formula was not equitable in the first place. The financial formula needs to be revised in order that provinces like Newfoundland will have a better opportunity to participate and finance the building of the road. If the government is going to continue to maintain the same financial formula it is simply penalizing those provinces which because of their geography or their economy have been less able to finance the building of the first trans-Canada highway than other provinces.
I think it is most unwise to ask other provinces to wait until the last mile of the first trans-Canada highway in the last province has been built. It is most unwise not to make other arrangements for financial participation in order to enable these poorer provinces to finish their section of the trans-Canada highway.

I should like to ask the minister to comment on the situation I raised with regard to the peculiar situation at Vancouver with respect to access roads and any offers of federal assistance that may have been turned down because of toll highways or toll bridges.

Before the minister replies I should also like to put a question to him. I have in my hand an advertisement which appeared in the Telegram of St. John's, Newfoundland, on Friday, August 14, 1959.
[Mr. Martin (Essex East).)

It is headed, "Charter for a New Deal for Newfoundland". In one corner it contains a picture of Mr. Malcolm Hollett, at that time leader of the Progressive Conservative party in Newfoundland, and it also contains the program of the provincial party that was put before the electors in the last provincial election. Point No. 10 is as follows:
Complete the trans-Canada highway on terms consistent with Newfoundland's needs and capacity to pay.
Then it goes on to say:
If a proper agreement, one that took due account of Newfoundland's needs and its low capacity to pay, had been entered into by the provincial Liberal government when they came to power 10 years ago the highway across Newfoundland could have been built and fully paved by now. Progressive Conservative leader Malcolm Hollett has talked with the Prime Minister, Mr. Diefenbaker, and with other ministers of the Diefenbaker cabinet, about the impossible position Newfoundland is in under the present trans-Canada highway contract. Mr. Hollett believes that "the Diefenbaker government is prepared to re-negotiate that useless agreement; . .. that the Diefenbaker government is prepared to give sympathetic consideration to the submission that the highway be completed entirely by the federal government."
This was the pledge on which the leader of the Progressive Conservative party in Newfoundland went to the country in August of last year. I realize I would be out of order to recall the circumstances, but hon. members will remember that Mr. Hollett was the express champion of the Prime Minister in connection with an attitude taken by the Prime Minister in this house which was not so popular in Newfoundland. Mr. Hollett is no longer a member of the legislature, although I believe he is still the leader of the Progressive Conservative party in Newfoundland. Mr. Hollett says in this statement:
Progressive Conservative Leader Malcolm Hollett has talked with the Prime Minister, Mr. Diefenbaker, and with other ministers of the Diefenbaker cabinet, about the impossible position Newfoundland is in under the present trans-Canada highway contract. Mr. Hollett believes "that the Diefenbaker government is prepared to re-negotiate that useless agreement.. . that the Diefenbaker government is prepared to give sympathetic consideration to the submission that the highway be completed entirely by the federal government."
This advertisement appeared on August 14. I do not expect the Minister of Public Works who, at the time this was written, I do not believe was a member of the cabinet, to tell me what actually did take place in these conversations between Mr. Hollett and the Prime Minister. However, I wanted to put this on the record today so the minister would have it before him and have an opportunity to ascertain what did take place in connection with the conversations and to ascertain whether or not Mr. Hollett was right in his contention that the Diefenbaker government

was prepared to re-negotiate this "useless agreement" as Mr. Hollett calls it and, if so, if the Diefenbaker government was prepared to carry out that undertaking given to Mr. Hollett. I put that on the record so that the minister will have an opportunity, when the committee next considers this matter, to give an answer, unless the minister is prepared to give an answer right away.
I want on the record an answer to my question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: For the sake of orderly debate, I was going to recognize the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka.
The minister was just getting up before the previous hon. member spoke to answer my question about the position of Vancouver.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: There are only five minutes to go before adjournment, and I could not possibly state the position with respect to Vancouver; I will take half an hour to answer the hon. member.

There are only five minutes before adjournment, but I will try to complete what I want to say in that time. There has been criticism during this debate about the slowness of the province of Ontario in completing its section of the trans-Canada highway. I think it is well recognized that the longest portion of the highway is in the province of Ontario through some of the most rugged country.
I should like to take, for example, the stretch of highway through the eastern Georgian bay area in the neighbourhood of the town of Parry Sound. During the last two years I have watched the progress of this section of the trans-Canada highway, as bridges have been built, sections of the road have been prepared and contracts have been let. The road is making good progress. It has not been easy work, but it has been progressing as rapidly as one could expect in view of the type of territory through which construction is proceeding and the bridges and other works which must be completed. I should like to say, in support of the resolution, that the building of this highway through the eastern Georgian bay area has opened up a tremendous section of the country to development.
A number of hon. members have mentioned the tourist trade that has developed as a result of the building of the trans-Canada highway. This particular section is no exception. As a result of the impetus provided by the building of this highway, the same Minister of Public Works has recently undertaken a dredging job in Key river area 79951-0-167
Business of the House
which will open up the area for boats and for pleasure craft, to which access is provided by the trans-Canada highway. A few years ago this highway did not go any further north than the village of Britt. Since then, it has been completed, in a partial state, through to Sudbury. This particular section of the highway is of great value in the development of this excellent recreational area. It is not yet completed and further time will be required. It is for this reason that the resolution is greatly appreciated because it does extend the time for completion of this section, in common with all the others that are being completed across the country.
May I call it six o'clock?
Progress reported.
I wonder if the leader of the house could possibly indicate the course of business right up to the Easter adjournment?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes. We will continue with the business as I outlined last night, that is, we will start with Bill No. S-26, an act to amend the National Energy Board Act. If that is completed we will continue with the resolution that was under discussion today concerning the Trans-Canada Highway Act and the other items of business that I outlined last night.
Would the minister mind repeating them, so they would be in the record?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The third item would be the resolution in the name of the minister of northern affairs, which is No. 11 on today's order paper, dealing with the Yukon Act; then after that, a resolution also in his name dealing with the Northwest Territories Act. This will occupy all the time tomorrow. Thursday night is the budget speech. Friday, we start with the resolution in the name of the Minister of Finance dealing with the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act. If that is completed on Friday we will continue with these items I have been talking about now.
Monday, April 4, would normally be a private members' day. I have already had consultations with hon. gentlemen on the other side and I suggested it might be advisable, in order to have a continuous budget debate and complete the budget debate by April 13, to transfer the private members' Monday from April 4 to April 25 so that there will be no loss of time whatsoever. If there is agreement to this course being followed, perhaps an order of the house could issue to

Business of the House
that effect. It would permit us to commence the budget debate on Monday, April 4 and carry it right through for the eight appointed days, ending on April 13 when the house would then rise for the Easter recess.
Mr. Speaker, I might say that as far as we are concerned we would be quite agreeable to that arrangement on the understanding that the budget debate would be continuous.
1 understand the leader of this party has indicated our agreement to the same arrangement.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Then perhaps this would be the appropriate time for the house to give unanimous consent and order that next Monday, private members' day, be deferred in favour of the budget debate, presumably until the Monday after Easter.
Yes, Monday, April 25.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes. Does the house agree to that course?
Agreed.
